title: The Inquisition, honestly
hook: church courts that used coercion and handed people to execution; John Paul II asked forgiveness

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rose and Martin, a garden hut and a broom. Your line was lima's saints. Who did you notice that your city tends to look past? Day one thousand two hundred forty-one.

A Sunday in Lent, in Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome. Pope John Paul II stands before a crucifix. One after another, cardinals step forward and name sins committed by members of the Church, and after each one the pope asks God's forgiveness. One confession is for sins committed in the service of truth: intolerance, and force used against others in the name of faith. The cardinal who reads it leads the Vatican office that grew out of the old Roman Inquisition. This path has been walking with the Dominicans: veritas, study, preaching, the rosary, Montesinos. Today it looks at the hardest part of the story, honestly.
screen: `A SUNDAY IN LENT, SAINT PETER'S.` → `SINS IN THE SERVICE OF TRUTH.` → `THE HARDEST PART, HONESTLY.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Inquisition comes from the Latin inquisitio, an inquiry, a legal investigation. It wasn't one court. In medieval Europe, popes appointed inquisitors to investigate heresy, and among them were friars, Dominicans and Franciscans. Later came the Spanish Inquisition, run under the Spanish crown, which pursued people whose families had converted from Judaism or Islam and who were suspected of keeping their old faith in secret. Then the Roman Inquisition. Here is what the courts did. They questioned people. They used coercion, and at times torture. And when someone was judged a heretic and wouldn't recant, the court handed them over to the civil authorities, who put them to death. The Church didn't light the fire, but it handed the person to the ones who did. Historians argue about the numbers, and popular stories sometimes inflate them. That argument doesn't change the core. The same order that preached veritas sometimes served this. So what does the Gospel say about force? When a Samaritan village refuses to welcome Jesus, James and John offer to call down fire from heaven on it. Luke says Jesus turns and rebukes them, and they go on to another village. And on the night he is arrested, when a disciple draws a sword, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Put up again thy sword into its place." That is why the confession in Saint Peter's matters. The Church said, in public, that people who believed they were serving the truth did it with force, and that this was sin. The sin wasn't explained away. Forgiveness was asked.
screen: `INQUISITIO: AN INQUIRY, A COURT.` · `MEDIEVAL, SPANISH, ROMAN.` · `COERCION, AND HANDING PEOPLE OVER TO DIE.` · `JESUS REBUKES THE CALL FOR FIRE.` · then, large: `PUT UP AGAIN THY SWORD INTO ITS PLACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for the victims of religious violence. Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind the people who stood before those courts, whose names we will never know. Jews and Muslims and their descendants, people judged heretics, people who simply said the wrong thing. Then widen it: everyone, of any faith or none, who has been hurt or killed by someone acting in the name of God. Don't try to explain it. Just hold them in silence. If you pray, you can say, "Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord," the Church's old prayer for the dead, or simply keep the silence. If you don't, let the quiet be your respect. The bell holds the time.
Inquisition. Church courts that investigated heresy, used coercion, and handed people over to be executed; a history the Church has publicly asked forgiveness for. Today's word.

Your line: forgiveness asked. Today, think of one time you were sure you were right and pushed too hard. If it's possible, ask that person's forgiveness, without explaining it away. Day one thousand two hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church has publicly confessed sins committed by its members in the use of force in the service of faith, notably in a Day of Pardon liturgy led by John Paul II; Catholics pray for the dead, including victims of religious violence, at Mass and with prayers such as 'Eternal rest'.
